items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Digital media is just traditional media in a different format." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Digital media is also searchable, copyable, interactive, networked and data-generating, which changes how it is produced, distributed, monetised and controlled.
items.markingKey: Digital media is also searchable, copyable, interactive, networked and data-generating, which changes how it is produced, distributed, monetised and controlled. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the business model of journalism has been disrupted by social media.
items.answer: Advertising moved to platforms such as Google and Meta, which offer targeted ads and audiences at scale, while news is shared for free on platforms, reducing newspapers' revenue and leading to closures of local newspapers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Advertising moved to platforms such as Google and Meta, which offer targeted ads and audiences at scale, while news is shared for free on platforms, reducing newspapers' revenue and leading to closures of local newspapers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an advertising model and a subscription model.
items.answer: A subscription model charges users directly for access (Netflix); an advertising model gives free access and earns money by selling audience attention to advertisers (YouTube free tier).
items.markingKey: A subscription model charges users directly for access (Netflix); an advertising model gives free access and earns money by selling audience attention to advertisers (YouTube free tier). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using VR exposure therapy as an example, explain immersive media in the health context.
items.answer: Clinicians use VR environments to treat phobias and PTSD by gradually exposing patients to feared situations in a controlled setting. Immersion allows safe, repeatable therapy that would be difficult in the real world.
items.markingKey: Context (Clinicians use VR environments to treat phobias and PTSD by gradually exposing patients to feared situations in a controlled setting.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: immersion allows safe, repeatable therapy that would be difficult in the real world. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to immersive media in the health context.

items.stem: "Traditional media no longer matters in the age of social media." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Television and established news outlets still set much of the agenda and much shared social-media content originates from professional news organisations.
items.markingKey: Television and established news outlets still set much of the agenda and much shared social-media content originates from professional news organisations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Spotify's payment model, explain how it illustrates the platform economy.
items.answer: Spotify pays rights holders roughly in proportion to their share of total streams (a "pro-rata" model); in 2024 it stopped paying for tracks with fewer than 1,000 annual streams. The platform's rules decide how revenue is shared, favouring popular artists and showing platform power over cultural income.
items.markingKey: Context (Spotify pays rights holders roughly in proportion to their share of total streams (a "pro-rata" model); in 2024 it stopped paying for tracks with fewer than 1,000 annual streams.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the platform's rules decide how revenue is shared, favouring popular artists and showing platform power over cultural income. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the platform economy.

items.stem: A video stream in standard definition (SD) uses about 3 Mbps. Calculate the data used in one hour, in gigabytes (1 GB = 1000 MB, 8 bits = 1 byte). A student watches 1 hour a day for 7 days on a mobile plan with a 50 GB allowance. Calculate the total data used and state whether it fits the plan.
items.answer: 1.35 GB per hour; 9.45 GB total – within the 50 GB allowance

items.stem: Using the Arab Spring (2010–2011) as an example, explain the interaction of social and mass media.
items.answer: Protesters in Tunisia and Egypt used Facebook, Twitter and YouTube to share images and organise; Al Jazeera amplified citizen footage. Citizen content reached global audiences through both social platforms and broadcast media, showing convergence rather than replacement.
items.markingKey: Context (Protesters in Tunisia and Egypt used Facebook, Twitter and YouTube to share images and organise; Al Jazeera amplified citizen footage.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: citizen content reached global audiences through both social platforms and broadcast media, showing convergence rather than replacement. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the interaction of social and mass media.

items.stem: A video gets 2,500,000 views; 60% are shown ads. Advertisers pay US$2 per 1,000 ad views (CPM), and the platform passes 55% of ad revenue to the creator. Calculate the creator's income.

A video stream in 720p HD uses about 3.5 Mbps. Calculate the data used in one hour, in gigabytes (1 GB = 1000 MB, 8 bits = 1 byte). A student watches 1 hour a day for 7 days on a mobile plan with a 50 GB allowance. Calculate the total data used and state whether it fits the plan.
items.answer: 1.575 GB per hour; 11.03 GB total – within the 50 GB allowance

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Participatory media has improved the quality of public information."
items.answer: Participatory media has widened information but not consistently improved its quality; it works best alongside professional journalism.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: more voices and first-hand evidence; faster reporting and accountability (George Floyd video). Arguments against: misinformation and lack of verification; loss of local journalism; algorithmic amplification of sensational content. Supported judgement: Participatory media has widened information but not consistently improved its quality; it works best alongside professional journalism.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that streaming platforms have been good for creators.
items.answer: Platforms widened access to audiences, but most creators gain little income; benefits are concentrated among the most popular.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: global distribution without labels or studios; new income streams (ads, fan funding). Arguments against: low pay per stream and unequal income; dependence on algorithms and changing rules; platforms capture much of the value. Supported judgement: Platforms widened access to audiences, but most creators gain little income; benefits are concentrated among the most popular. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Immersive media such as VR will replace traditional screen-based media." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Immersive media will grow in specific uses (training, gaming, therapy) but is unlikely to replace screens soon.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: deeper engagement and presence; large investment (Meta, Apple Vision Pro 2024). Arguments against: headsets are expensive, uncomfortable and isolating; adoption has been slower than predicted; screens remain convenient and social. Supported judgement: Immersive media will grow in specific uses (training, gaming, therapy) but is unlikely to replace screens soon. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.
